patent: Filed 1913-10-29 and issued 1914-10-06 to Edwin H. Armstrong of Yonkers, N.Y.; Armstrong worked out the circuit in 1912 while at Columbia University. It is his regenerative (feedback) receiver. The three-electrode audion of Lee de Forest (US 879,532) serves as the detector, and part of the amplified high-frequency current in its plate ("wing") circuit is returned to the grid circuit, so the received oscillations build up and the telephone signal grows many times. The text names three ways of returning energy: tuning the wing circuit to the received wave (L', C^{3}); capacity common to both circuits (the audion's own electrode capacity, the telephone cords, condensers); and an inductance in the filament lead shared by both circuits (the telephones, a coil, or a transformer that steps up its voltage). Gain rises until the audion becomes a generator of high frequency oscillations; the operator sets L' and C' just below that point. The same feedback carried past that point is the vacuum-tube oscillator. Armstrong described the work in "Some Recent Developments in the Audion Receiver", Proceedings of the IRE, 1915. De Forest later claimed priority for the feedback circuit, and after long litigation the US Supreme Court ruled for de Forest (Radio Corp. of America v. Radio Engineering Laboratories, 293 U.S. 1, 1934).

figs.1: Grid circuit: S and L lead through grid condenser C' to grid G; C shunts S and L to the grounded line. From tap O the grid circuit returns through auto-transformer T and C^{2} to the grounded side of S. Wing circuit: battery through L' (tuned by C^{3}) to wing W, then from filament F down through telephones R and the section of T above tap O, back to the battery; C^{4} spans the battery. R and the upper section of T are the part common to both circuits. C^{5} (left) bridges R and the whole of T; C^{6} (right) bridges R and the section of T above O. The small battery and rheostat X at the bulb heat the filament. An arrow drawn through a part marks it as continuously variable.
figs.2: The aerial A is tapped onto coil L, used as an auto-transformer in place of P and S, and onto an unlettered coil at left whose foot is grounded; condenser C joins the foot of L to the grounded line. Telephones R lie between the filament F and junction O, in the lead common to both circuits. The wing circuit runs from the battery through a tap on L' to W, with C^{4} across the battery. There is no transformer T and no C^{2}, C^{3}, C^{5} or C^{6}.
figs.3: Wing circuit tuned by variable inductance L', but the telephones R, shunted by an unlettered variable condenser, sit on the bottom line to the right of the point where the grid circuit returns to the filament, so they carry wing current only and no inductance is shared by the two circuits. C^{4} spans the battery.
figs.4: Wing circuit not tuned: a plain wire runs from W to the battery. Telephones R are in the filament lead, between the filament and the junction where the grid circuit returns, so they are common to both circuits and their inductance supplies the maintaining electromotive-force. The filament rheostat is drawn but not lettered.
figs.5: Telephones R are moved into the wing circuit (right-hand vertical, between W and the battery), and variable inductance L^{2}, shunted by variable condenser C^{5}, takes their place between the filament and junction O. The grid condenser is lettered C on this sheet, not C'. The wing circuit has no tuning inductance.
figs.6: A two-coil transformer, drawn as two unlettered windings hanging from the filament junction, replaces the auto-transformer. The right-hand winding (primary) is tapped into the wing circuit toward the battery; the left-hand winding (secondary) is tapped by the return lead from S. C^{5} bridges the secondary section and C^{6} the primary section. R, shunted by an unlettered variable condenser, is in the wing circuit between the battery and L'; C^{4} spans the battery. The aerial and the grid condenser are not lettered.

parts.C': Grid condenser. The grid rectifies, and the charge it collects is held on C'; the text says the charge outlasts each wave train because its discharge path has high resistance.
parts.C: In Fig. 5 the letter C stands at the series grid condenser, the position lettered C' in the other figures.
parts.T: Single tapped winding. The section above tap O, in series with the telephones, carries wing current; the grid circuit passes through the whole winding to C^{2}, so the voltage across that section is stepped up (the text gives a 2 to 1 ratio).
parts.R: Headphones. Where they lie in the lead common to both circuits (Figs. 1, 2, 4), their inductance supplies the maintaining electromotive-force.
parts.X: Filament rheostat, set for filament temperature.
parts.L': Wing-circuit tuning inductance; with C' the operator's main adjustment (about 10,000 microhenries in the text's example).

glossary.def: De Forest's three-electrode vacuum tube (filament, grid, plate), the forerunner of the triode; drawn here as a bulb with a hairpin filament F, a zigzag grid G and a plate W.
The patent's word for the audion's plate (anode); the wing circuit is the plate circuit.
The tuned input circuit that carries the received oscillations to the grid; the two circuits are interlinked by sharing the filament connection.
Positive feedback of amplified signal from the output circuit back to the input circuit; the patent does not use the word.
The voltage induced across an inductance when the current through it falls; it acts in the same direction as the battery and, when the inductance is shared, charges the grid condenser further.
Capacitor; "capacity" is used both for a capacitor and for capacitance.
A single winding with a tap, one section serving as primary and the whole as secondary.
Radio channels were then given by wavelength; 1800 meters is about 167 kHz, 2000 meters 150 kHz.
Units of capacitance and inductance; .00025 microfarads is 250 pF.
